newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE - Irish farmers seen voting for opposition parties.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Irish farmers seen voting for opposition parties.

text.p: Farmer John Crowley opened the dust-encrusted window of his tractor, thought a moment and then spat on the parched ground.
"Who will I vote for on Friday? I'll vote for an honest politician who understands the problems farmers face. But you'll have to find me an honest politician first," he said.

According to opinion polls, farmers like Crowley will back the opposition Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrats alliance in Friday's election and oust the government of Prime Minister John Bruton and his three-party rainbow coalition.

But the polls indicate that farmers, like many of the electorate, will vote tactically using the proportional representation system which allows them to list all competing candidates in order of preference.

This could lead to a hung parliament with neither of the two major blocs able to form a government without the support of small political parties, such as the National Party, a small "Family Values" party outside the political mainstream.

"That National Party woman, Theresa Heaney. She's sound I'd say," said Crowley, conferring on his near neighbour something close to a compliment in the tight-lipped and sparse language employed by the rural population of West Cork.
Heaney, 33, dresses like a Sunday school teacher, talks like an evangelist and is a member of a small pro-Life grouping that is fielding 16 candidates in the election.

If her party came to power it would immediately reopen the most divisive issues in Irish society -- abortion and divorce -- and fight to reinstate the hold of the Roman Catholic church on daily life, including the running of schools.
It would also pay housewives to stay at home, mind the children and play the foundation stone for the family.

"We stand for all the values that this government and the previous government and all the political parties have ignored," Heaney told Reuters on the doorstep of a cottage in her native village, 200 miles (300 km) from the capital, Dublin.

"Divorce and abortion are abominations. They are un-Irish. The family is the most important thing in Irish life and it's families that are being torn apart because no-one is standing up for the values they cherish," she said.
CONTRAST BETWEEN RURAL AND URBAN VOTERS

Last year Ireland voted by less than one percentage point to legalise divorce, which was outlawed in the country's founding constitution. Abortion can only be carried out in Ireland if the life of the expectant mother is threatened.

Bruton's coalition of his own Fine Gael, the Labour party and Democratic Left and Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail and its ally have all steered clear of the abortion issue for fear of opening up the deep divisions in Irish life.

They run, according to the result of the divorce referendum, along the fault lines of the society between voters in the rural areas and those in towns, where about half of Ireland's 3.5 million people live.

"A recent opinion poll showed that 72 percent of Irish people want a new referendum on abortion. The one we had in 1992 allowed it to be carried out in Ireland. It's shameful," Heaney said. "As for divorce. That was a disgrace."

Last year the Supreme Court ruled that Bruton's government had abused its position in using state money to print posters urging the electorate to legalise divorce to give separated couples the chance to remarry and rebuild their lives.

Heaney says the ruling made the referendum invalid and wants it held again. There are many like her in the Irish countryside, where "Vote No. Don't Break up the family" posters still cling to the occasional telegraph pole and barbed wire fence.

Crowley does not want to talk about either issue. His problems are the current drought, the Mad Cow disease scare which has hit Irish beef exports and his pocket, and the tumbling Irish pound, which has raised his import costs.
Bruton, whose father had a large farm, is simply unaware of the problems the average Irish farmer faces, he says.

But Fianna Fail, he says, understand the problems of the small farmer. "How can John Bruton, who is a big farmer and has hundreds upon hundreds of acres possibly understand what it is like to work from dawn to dusk for a pittance," he asked.

Like many voters he is scathing about Bruton's major coalition ally, the Labour party of Foreign Minister Dick Spring, who effectively brought down the previous Fianna Fail government by pulling out of a coalition.
Labour threw its weight behind Bruton, and opinion polls say that it will lose its balance of power and see its seats in parliament trimmed by a third to around 20.

Last week Fianna Fail sent Spring a poster with a picture of a cow on it and a sign saying: "This is a cow." The gesture was supposed to highlight Labour's drift to urban votes, especially in middle class Dublin.
"I was waiting for a call from Spring last week," Crowley said as he climbed back into his tractor. "I was going to explain to him what that four-legged black and white creature was."
